1.7 Geoprocessing with sf

Buffering the cycling paths
The cycling paths are first transformed to SVY21 so a buffer can be measured in metres.

cyclingpath <- st_transform(
  cyclingpath, crs = 3414)

The next cell creates a five-metre buffer around each path.

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(
  cyclingpath, dist=5, nQuadSegs = 30)

The buffer area can be added with base R syntax.

buffer_cycling$AREA <- st_area(buffer_cycling)

The tutorial then shows the equivalent dplyr approach.

buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%
  mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))


sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

4989654 [m^2]




Clipping the buffer to Tampines West

mpsz_selected <- mpsz %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST") 


buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(
  buffer_cycling, mpsz_selected)


plot(st_geometry(buffer_cycling_selected))

Part 2: Choropleth mapping
This section follows Chapter 2. It prepares Singapore population data and maps the dependency ratio by planning subzone.

2.1 Packages

pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse, rvest)



2.2 Importing the subzone boundaries
The Master Plan 2019 KML is imported and transformed to SVY21.

mpsz <- st_read("chap02/data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

The KML stores its attributes in HTML. This function retrieves one requested field.

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}


mpsz <- mpsz %>%
  mutate(
    REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())

2.3 Preparing the population table

popdata <- read_csv("chap02/data/aspatial/respopagesextod2024.csv")

The age groups are combined into young, economically active and aged populations. The dependency ratio compares young and aged residents with the economically active group.

popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup()%>%
  pivot_wider(names_from=AG, 
              values_from=POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         +rowSums(.[12])) %>%
mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11])+
rowSums(.[13:15]))%>%
mutate(`AGED`=rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
mutate(`TOTAL`=rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%  
mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
/`ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, 
       `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, 
       `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)

The place names are changed to uppercase to match the boundary attributes. Rows without an economically active population are removed.

popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ), 
          .funs = list(toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)



2.4 Joining population and boundary data

mpsz_pop2024 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2024,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))


write_rds(mpsz_pop2024, "chap02/data/rds/mpsz_pop2024.rds")



2.5 Quick choropleth map
qtm() provides a quick first view of the dependency ratio.

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2024, 
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")








The tutorial then builds a complete map in one cell.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authorithy (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))










2.6 Building a choropleth step by step
The next five cells add the fill and borders gradually.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons()









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60",
             lwd = 0.1,
             lty = "dashed")










2.7 Comparing classification methods
Quantile classes place a similar number of subzones in each class.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Equal intervals divide the numeric range into classes of the same width.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
 0.0000  0.6730  0.7324  0.7595  0.8109 10.0000      94 


Custom breaks can be supplied directly.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










2.8 Choosing colour schemes

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Adding a minus sign reverses the palette.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










2.9 Adding map elements

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))








The legend is positioned automatically inside the map.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_pos_auto_in() +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))










2.10 Map styles

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) + 
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + 
  tmap_style("natural")









tmap_style("white")



2.11 Small multiple maps
The first method maps the young and aged populations in one tmap call.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) + 
  tm_polygons(
    fill = c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
    fill.legend = 
      tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in(
        "right", "bottom")),
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal", 
      n = 5,
      values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")








The second method creates two maps and arranges them side by side.

youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+ 
  tm_polygons(fill = "YOUNG",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                  item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of young population")
                
agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+ 
  tm_polygons(fill = "AGED",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
              style = "quantile", 
              values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of aged population")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp=1, ncol=2)








The dependency ratio can also be faceted by region.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile",
            values = "brewer.blues")) + 
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            nrow = 2, 
            ncols = 3,
            free.coords=TRUE, 
            drop.units=TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = TRUE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"), 
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










2.12 Mapping a selected region

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend()) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








A box plot is added as a chart inside the map.

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(),
              fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)








The next map highlights dependency-ratio outliers in red.

mpsz_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")

stats <- boxplot.stats(mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY)

outlier_vals <- stats$out

outlier_sf <- mpsz_selected[mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tm_shape(mpsz_selected) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile", 
            values = "brewer.blues"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(),
          fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_text("SUBZONE_N", col = "red", size = 0.7) +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)










2.13 Interactive maps
The first interactive map focuses on the Central Region and highlights the same outliers.

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(region_selected, 
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name" = "SUBZONE_N", 
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2)





tmap_mode("plot")

The final map limits the available zoom levels.

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")

tm_shape(region_selected, 
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name" = "SUBZONE_N", 
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(12,14))





tmap_mode("plot")

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
section: Part 1: First-order spatial point pattern analysis
text:
Part 1: First-order spatial point pattern analysis
First-order analysis describes where childcare services are concentrated. I begin by preparing the data, then use the Clark–Evans test and kernel density estimation (KDE).

1.1 Packages

pacman::p_load(sf, terra, spatstat, 
               tmap, rvest, tidyverse)



1.2 Importing and preparing the geospatial data
The analysis uses the Master Plan 2019 subzone boundaries and Child Care Services data from data.gov.sg. The current childcare download is GeoJSON, so I prepared local KML and RDS copies with the same records and filenames expected by the tutorial.

mpsz_sf <- st_read("chap04/data/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml") %>% 
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>% st_transform(crs = 3414)

Reading layer `MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML' from data source 
  `D:\smu\study\GIS\chap04\data\MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml' 
  using driver `KML'
Simple feature collection with 332 features and 2 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84


The KML stores the boundary attributes in an HTML table. This function extracts one named field from that table.

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}


mpsz_sf <- mpsz_sf %>%
  mutate(
    REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())

The tutorial removes three offshore areas before creating the Singapore study window.

mpsz_cl <- mpsz_sf %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N != "SOUTHERN GROUP",
         PLN_AREA_N != "WESTERN ISLANDS",
         PLN_AREA_N != "NORTH-EASTERN ISLANDS")


write_rds(mpsz_cl, 
          "chap04/data/mpsz_cl.rds")


mpsz_cl <- read_rds("chap04/data/mpsz_cl.rds")

The childcare locations are also transformed to Singapore SVY21 (EPSG:3414), whose units are metres.

childcare_sf <- st_read("chap04/data/ChildCareServices.kml") %>% 
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

Reading layer `ChildCareServices' from data source 
  `D:\smu\study\GIS\chap04\data\ChildCareServices.kml' using driver `KML'
Simple feature collection with 1925 features and 2 fields
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6878 ymin: 1.247759 xmax: 103.9897 ymax: 1.462134
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84




1.3 Mapping the two datasets
The first map checks that the childcare points and subzone boundaries share the same spatial extent.

tm_shape(mpsz_cl) +
  tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(childcare_sf)+
  tm_dots()








The interactive version makes it possible to zoom and inspect individual points. The final line returns tmap to static mode.

tmap_mode('view')
tm_shape(childcare_sf)+
  tm_dots()




tmap_mode('plot')



1.4 Converting the data for spatstat
spatstat represents points as a ppp object and the study area as an owin object.

childcare_ppp <- as.ppp(childcare_sf)


class(childcare_ppp)

[1] "ppp"



summary(childcare_ppp)

Marked planar point pattern:  1925 points
Average intensity 2.417323e-06 points per square unit

*Pattern contains duplicated points*

Coordinates are given to 11 decimal places

Mark variables: Name, Description
Summary:
        Name         Description  
 Length   :1925   Length   :1925  
 N.unique :1572   N.unique :   1  
 N.blank  :   0   N.blank  :   0  
 Min.nchar:   9   Min.nchar:  19  
 Max.nchar:  74   Max.nchar:  19  

Window: rectangle = [11810.03, 45404.24] x [25596.33, 49300.88] units
                    (33590 x 23700 units)
Window area = 796335000 square units



sg_owin <- as.owin(mpsz_cl)


class(sg_owin)

[1] "owin"



plot(sg_owin)








Only childcare points inside the Singapore observation window are retained.

childcareSG_ppp = childcare_ppp[sg_owin]


childcareSG_ppp

Marked planar point pattern: 1925 points
Mark variables: Name, Description 
window: polygonal boundary
enclosing rectangle: [2667.54, 55941.94] x [21448.47, 50256.33] units




1.5 Clark–Evans nearest-neighbour test
The Clark–Evans test compares observed nearest-neighbour spacing with complete spatial randomness (CSR). An R value below 1 indicates that points are closer together than expected.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"))


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)


The Monte Carlo version compares the observed pattern with 99 simulated random patterns.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion="sg_owin",
                alternative=c("clustered"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.53532, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)


Both tests provide evidence that childcare services are clustered rather than randomly distributed.


1.6 Kernel density estimation
KDE turns the individual service locations into a continuous density surface. The first estimate uses Diggle’s automatic bandwidth and an edge correction.

kde_SG_diggle <- density(
  childcareSG_ppp,
  sigma=bw.diggle,
  edge=TRUE,
  kernel="gaussian") 


plot(kde_SG_diggle)









summary(kde_SG_diggle)

real-valued pixel image
128 x 128 pixel array (ny, nx)
enclosing rectangle: [2667.538, 55941.94] x [21448.47, 50256.33] units
dimensions of each pixel: 416 x 225.0614 units
Image is defined on a subset of the rectangular grid
Subset area = 669941961.12249 square units
Subset area fraction = 0.437
Pixel values (inside window):
    range = [-6.584123e-21, 3.063698e-05]
    integral = 1927.788
    mean = 2.877545e-06


The very small values are services per square metre. The selected bandwidth can be inspected directly.

bw <- bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp)
bw

   sigma 
295.9712 


Rescaling the point pattern from metres to kilometres makes the density values easier to read.

childcareSG_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(
  childcareSG_ppp, 1000, "km")


kde_childcareSG_km <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
                              sigma=bw.diggle,
                              edge=TRUE,
                              kernel="gaussian")


plot(kde_childcareSG_km)








The map pattern is unchanged, but the values are now expressed per square kilometre.

Comparing automatic bandwidth methods
The following cells calculate the four bandwidth selectors used in the tutorial.

bw.CvL(childcareSG_ppp_km)

   sigma 
4.357209 



bw.scott(childcareSG_ppp_km)

 sigma.x  sigma.y 
2.159749 1.396455 



bw.ppl(childcareSG_ppp_km)

   sigma 
0.378997 



bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp_km)

    sigma 
0.2959712 


A smaller bandwidth preserves more local detail, while a larger bandwidth produces a smoother regional pattern.

kde_childcareSG.ppl <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
                               sigma=bw.ppl, 
                               edge=TRUE,
                               kernel="gaussian")
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_km, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_childcareSG.ppl, main = "bw.ppl")










Comparing kernel shapes
With the same bandwidth, the four kernels distribute weight around each location differently.

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="gaussian"), 
     main="Gaussian")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="epanechnikov"), 
     main="Epanechnikov")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="quartic"), 
     main="Quartic")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km, 
             sigma=0.2959712, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="disc"), 
     main="Disc")











1.7 Fixed and adaptive KDE
The fixed estimate applies a 0.6 km bandwidth everywhere.

kde_childcareSG_fb <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
                              sigma=0.6, 
                              edge=TRUE,
                              kernel="gaussian")
plot(kde_childcareSG_fb)








The adaptive estimate changes its smoothing according to the local point pattern.

kde_childcareSG_ab <- adaptive.density(
  childcareSG_ppp_km, 
  method="kernel")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab)









par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_fb, main = "Fixed bandwidth")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")










1.8 Converting the KDE surface to a raster map
The im density surface is converted to a SpatRaster so it can be mapped with tmap.

kde_childcareSG_bw_terra <- rast(kde_childcareSG_km)


class(kde_childcareSG_bw_terra)

[1] "SpatRaster"
attr(,"package")
[1] "terra"



kde_childcareSG_bw_terra

class       : SpatRaster
size        : 128, 128, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 0.4162063, 0.2250614  (x, y)
extent      : 2.667538, 55.94194, 21.44847, 50.25633  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : 
source(s)   : memory

min value   :        -0
max value   : 30.636981

The raster does not carry a coordinate reference system automatically, so the tutorial assigns EPSG:3414.

crs(kde_childcareSG_bw_terra) <- "EPSG:3414"


kde_childcareSG_bw_terra

class       : SpatRaster
size        : 128, 128, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 0.4162063, 0.2250614  (x, y)
extent      : 2.667538, 55.94194, 21.44847, 50.25633  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414)
source(s)   : memory
name        :     lyr.1
min value   :        -0
max value   : 30.636981

tm_shape(kde_childcareSG_bw_terra) + 
  tm_raster(col.scale = 
              tm_scale_continuous(
                values = "viridis"),
            col.legend = tm_legend(
            title = "Density values",
            title.size = 0.7,
            text.size = 0.7,
            bg.color = "white",
            bg.alpha = 0.7,
            position = tm_pos_in(
              "right", "bottom"),
            frame = TRUE)) +
  tm_graticules(labels.size = 0.7) +
  tm_compass() +
  tm_layout(scale = 1.0)










1.9 Analysis by planning area
The tutorial compares Punggol, Tampines, Choa Chu Kang and Jurong West.

pg <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "PUNGGOL")
tm <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "TAMPINES")
ck <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "CHOA CHU KANG")
jw <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "JURONG WEST")


par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(st_geometry(pg), main = "Ponggol")
plot(st_geometry(tm), main = "Tampines")
plot(st_geometry(ck), main = "Choa Chu Kang")
plot(st_geometry(jw), main = "Jurong West")








Each planning area is converted to its own observation window.

pg_owin = as.owin(pg)
tm_owin = as.owin(tm)
ck_owin = as.owin(ck)
jw_owin = as.owin(jw)

The Singapore point pattern is clipped to each window.

childcare_pg_ppp = childcare_ppp[pg_owin]
childcare_tm_ppp = childcare_ppp[tm_owin]
childcare_ck_ppp = childcare_ppp[ck_owin]
childcare_jw_ppp = childcare_ppp[jw_owin]


childcare_pg_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(childcare_pg_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_tm_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(childcare_tm_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_ck_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(childcare_ck_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_jw_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(childcare_jw_ppp, 1000, "km")


par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(unmark(childcare_pg_ppp.km), 
  main="Punggol")
plot(unmark(childcare_tm_ppp.km), 
  main="Tampines")
plot(unmark(childcare_ck_ppp.km), 
  main="Choa Chu Kang")
plot(unmark(childcare_jw_ppp.km), 
  main="Jurong West")








The Clark–Evans tests below compare Choa Chu Kang and Tampines.

clarkevans.test(childcare_ck_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion=NULL,
                alternative=c("two.sided"),
                nsim=999)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

section: Beyond the tutorial: comparison and sensitivity analysis
text:
Beyond the tutorial: comparison and sensitivity analysis
The tutorial establishes whether each point pattern departs from CSR. The following analysis asks two additional questions:

How do the four planning areas compare after accounting for their different land areas?
Do services recorded at identical coordinates materially affect the clustering results?


3.1 Comparing density and nearest-neighbour structure
One point is retained for every service record in the original patterns. A second set of patterns retains only one point at each unique coordinate. This is a sensitivity check, not a replacement for the source data: co-located records represent real services, but they do not represent separate physical locations.

area_patterns <- list(
  "Punggol" = childcare_pg_ppp,
  "Tampines" = childcare_tm_ppp,
  "Choa Chu Kang" = childcare_ck_ppp,
  "Jurong West" = childcare_jw_ppp
)

unique_location_pattern <- function(point_pattern) {
  unique_coordinate <- !duplicated(
    cbind(point_pattern$x, point_pattern$y)
  )
  point_pattern[unique_coordinate]
}

area_comparison <- imap_dfr(area_patterns, function(point_pattern, area_name) {
  unique_pattern <- unique_location_pattern(point_pattern)

  original_test <- clarkevans.test(
    point_pattern,
    correction = "none",
    alternative = "two.sided"
  )

  unique_test <- clarkevans.test(
    unique_pattern,
    correction = "none",
    alternative = "two.sided"
  )

  area_km2 <- area.owin(Window(point_pattern)) / 1e6

  tibble(
    planning_area = area_name,
    area_km2 = area_km2,
    services = npoints(point_pattern),
    unique_locations = npoints(unique_pattern),
    services_per_km2 = npoints(point_pattern) / area_km2,
    original_R = unname(original_test$statistic),
    unique_location_R = unname(unique_test$statistic),
    unique_location_p = unique_test$p.value
  )
})

area_comparison |>
  transmute(
    `Planning area` = planning_area,
    `Area (km²)` = round(area_km2, 2),
    Services = services,
    `Unique locations` = unique_locations,
    `Services per km²` = round(services_per_km2, 2),
    `Original R` = round(original_R, 3),
    `Unique-location R` = round(unique_location_R, 3),
    `Unique-location p` = format.pval(
      unique_location_p,
      digits = 3,
      eps = 0.001
    )
  ) |>

3.2 Effect of shared coordinates
The comparison chart shows how the Clark–Evans ratio changes when repeated coordinates are collapsed. Values below one indicate shorter nearest-neighbour distances than expected under CSR.

Clark–Evans R before and after retaining one service per unique coordinate.




The sensitivity test changes the interpretation for Choa Chu Kang. Its original result is \(R = 0.841\) and rejects CSR, but the unique-location pattern gives \(R = 1.002\) with \(p = 0.975\). Its nearest-neighbour evidence of clustering is therefore largely explained by services sharing the same coordinates.
Tampines remains significantly clustered after the same adjustment (\(R = 0.752\), \(p < 0.001\)). This indicates clustering between distinct service locations, rather than only within shared addresses. Jurong West shows the same robust pattern, while Punggol no longer rejects CSR after repeated coordinates are collapsed.
These results also clarify the second-order plots. Tampines leaves the G, F, K and L envelopes, supporting clustering across several spatial relationships and distances. Choa Chu Kang gives mixed evidence: F remains inside its CSR envelope, while the strongest G and L departures occur at approximately one and two metres. Those near-zero departures are consistent with co-located service records, so a broad clustering claim for Choa Chu Kang should be made cautiously.


3.3 Comparable KDE hotspots
The planning-area KDEs above use independently selected bandwidths, which are useful for examining each area but not ideal for comparing peak values. The following analysis applies the same 0.6 km Gaussian bandwidth to all four patterns.

find_fixed_hotspot <- function(point_pattern, area_name) {
  point_pattern_km <- rescale.ppp(point_pattern, 1000, "km")

  density_surface <- density(
    point_pattern_km,
    sigma = 0.6,
    edge = TRUE,
    kernel = "gaussian"
  )

  peak_cell <- which(
    density_surface$v == max(density_surface$v, na.rm = TRUE),
    arr.ind = TRUE
  )[1, ]

  tibble(
    planning_area = area_name,
    peak_density = max(density_surface$v, na.rm = TRUE),
    easting = density_surface$xcol[peak_cell[2]] * 1000,
    northing = density_surface$yrow[peak_cell[1]] * 1000
  )
}

hotspot_points <- imap_dfr(
  area_patterns,
  ~ find_fixed_hotspot(.x, .y)
) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("easting", "northing"), crs = 3414)

hotspot_comparison <- st_join(
  hotspot_points,
  mpsz_cl |> select(SUBZONE_N),
  join = st_within
) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  transmute(
    `Planning area` = planning_area,
    `Peak subzone` = str_to_title(SUBZONE_N),
    `Peak density (services per km²)` = round(peak_density, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(`Peak density (services per km²)`))

With a common smoothing scale, Taman Jurong has the highest estimated local concentration among these four areas, followed by Peng Siang, Punggol Field and Tampines West. These are concentration hotspots, not measures of service adequacy: the dataset records service locations but does not provide enrolment capacity or demand.


3.4 Overall conclusion
The additional comparison shows that the number of services, service density and spatial clustering should not be treated as interchangeable. Choa Chu Kang has the highest area-normalised density, but its nearest-neighbour clustering disappears when shared coordinates are collapsed. Tampines has a lower area-normalised density yet retains strong first- and second-order evidence of clustering between distinct locations. The most defensible conclusion is therefore that Tampines exhibits broader spatial clustering, while Choa Chu Kang’s original nearest-neighbour result is sensitive to co-located records.

Counts, density surfaces and point-pattern tests describe different parts of the same story. The most useful conclusion is therefore not simply which area has more services, but whether its apparent clustering remains after area size and repeated locations are considered.

       main=paste("KDE at month",i))
}








The density surfaces help distinguish a real concentration from a pile of overlapping dots. In July and August, the stronger concentration is mainly in the west and north. It then shifts towards the south and east from September to November, with the widest and strongest surface in October. By December, the density falls sharply.

section: 9. Checking clustering across space and time
text:
9. Checking clustering across space and time
The density maps show where activity is stronger. I now use a space-time K-function to check whether pairs of fires occur closer together than expected under spatial and temporal independence.

9.1 Creating the space-time point object
First, I extract the projected coordinates.

coords <- st_coordinates(fire_sf)

I combine the coordinates with the day of year.

fire_df <- data.frame(
  x = coords[, 1],
  y = coords[, 2],
  t = fire_sf$`DayofYear`)

The data frame is then converted to the format used by stpp.

fire_stpp <- as.3dpoints(fire_df)


class(fire_stpp)

[1] "stpp"


The 3D plot uses the two horizontal axes for location and the vertical axis for day of year.

plot(fire_stpp)








The left panel shows the spatial pattern. On the right, the cumulative line rises slowly early in the year and much faster after about day 200, confirming that most detections occurred later in 2023.


9.2 Computing the space-time K-function

kbb_stik <- STIKhat(fire_stpp)

To make the result easier to interpret, I subtract the value expected under independence from the observed K-function. Positive values mean there are more nearby event pairs than expected.

k_difference <- kbb_stik$Khat - kbb_stik$Ktheo

filled.contour(
  x = kbb_stik$dist / 1000,
  y = kbb_stik$times,
  z = k_difference,
  color.palette = hcl.colors,
  xlab = "Spatial distance (km)",
  ylab = "Time difference (days)",
  main = "Observed K-function minus expected value"
)








The difference is positive across the distances and time gaps shown, from about 2.9 to 43.5 kilometres and 6 to 87 days. This means the data contain more nearby fire pairs than an independent pattern would produce. Together with the density maps, it supports the view that the fires are clustered in both place and time.
This is still a descriptive comparison rather than a formal significance test. Simulation envelopes would be needed before making a stronger statistical claim.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
10. Discussion
The monthly and daily views tell a consistent story. Fire activity is limited early in 2023, begins to rise around July, and is strongest from August to October. The main concentration also moves: it is more visible in the west and north during July and August, before becoming stronger in the south and east from September to November.
The improved daily KDE makes that change easier to follow because it smooths over about 19 days while retaining more local spatial detail. The K-function comparison points in the same direction, showing more nearby fire pairs than expected under independence. The analysis can show when and where concentrations appear, but it does not identify their cause; weather, land cover, land management, and detection conditions would need separate data.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
1. Choosing the direction
Both options in the assignment brief could support an interesting analysis. The forest-fire option would require selecting a Kalimantan regency and carefully separating satellite detections from individual fires within the available part of 2026. For this exercise, I prefer road accident records in Greater Bangkok during 2022. The downloaded file contains observations in every month of that year, and its English fields make the recording process easier to inspect than the Thai-language 2024 alternative.
The attraction is not simply finding the largest patch of dots. A busy road can have many crashes because many people use it. A quiet patch on the map could also reflect roads that this reporting system does not cover. I therefore start with recorded crash occurrence, rather than claiming to measure the chance that a road user will be involved in a crash.
My main question is:

How does the occurrence of recorded road accidents vary across Greater Bangkok and through 2022, and how much of the apparent pattern depends on the way the data were recorded?

Later, I will ask whether accidents close together in space also occur close together in time, after accounting for the observed spatial and temporal distributions.

The plan, and why this order makes sense








Stage
What I will do
What would make the result useful?




1. Establish the evidence — this instalment
Define the region and event; audit dates, coordinates and duplicates; map the retained records; examine timing and missing locations.
Every inclusion and exclusion is traceable, and initial observations distinguish missing data from absence of crashes.


2. Estimate concentrations and examine interaction — later
Compare planar KDE at 1, 2 and 4 km bandwidths in the same metre-based projection. Then examine space-time close-pair counts or a space-time K summary using simulated timestamp permutations.
Identify spatial features that survive reasonable smoothing choices, and assess space-time association against an explicit reference model.


3. Check the conclusions and communicate them — later
Assess sensitivity to coincident records, distance/time thresholds and the temporal permutation scheme; integrate results and planning implications; prepare the revealjs summary.
Explain what the evidence supports, what it cannot establish, and which conclusions are stable enough to communicate.



For the later simulations, I plan to keep the observed locations fixed and permute the observed timestamps. This asks whether location and time are independent conditional on these recorded locations and times. It preserves the road-shaped spatial support better than scattering simulated crashes uniformly across the entire land area. It still assumes timestamps are exchangeable across locations; different local seasonal patterns could challenge that assumption. I will examine a within-month permutation as a sensitivity check. Initial choices of 0.5, 1 and 2 km, and 1, 7 and 30 days, are exploratory scales, not predefined safety thresholds. A seed will be set before randomisation; 999 permutations are planned for the final comparison.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
2. Data and study design

2.1 Sources and acquisition
I downloaded the two required core datasets. No extra contextual layers are used at this stage.



Dataset
Source and coverage
Version and limitation




Road accident records
Thailand Road Accident 2019–2022, an English-language compilation attributed to Thailand’s Ministry of Transport. National coverage, with 2022 selected here.
Kaggle version 1, updated 19 August 2023; listed as CC0. This is a previously processed compilation, not the original reporting database.


Provincial boundaries
geoBoundaries gbOpen, Thailand ADM1, derived from OpenStreetMap/Wambacher.
Pinned release commit 9469f09, boundary ID THA-ADM1-36821470; represents 2017, built in 2023; ODbL 1.0. The geometry is an operational study boundary, not a verified 2022 legal boundary.



The Ministry of Transport’s own catalogue describes its accident data as covering highways, rural roads and expressways. This is an important scope limit: I do not treat this file as a census of every crash on every Bangkok street.
The core files were accessed on 11 September 2026. The download script retrieves pinned data versions and records file sizes, access time and SHA-256 checksums in a source manifest. The metadata snapshot preserves the source descriptions at acquisition. Raw downloads stay in the project’s ignored data/take-home-01/raw/ folder. They can be retrieved again with:

# Run once from the project root before rendering this report.
source("scripts/download-take-home-01.R")



2.2 Defining a point event
One point represents one reported accident record identified by acc_code. It does not represent one vehicle or one injured person. Fatality and injury totals remain attributes, rather than extra points at the same location.

Exact duplicate rows are removed and counted. Accident identifiers are then checked for repetition; conflicting records with the same identifier would require review before continuing.
Different identifiers at the same coordinates are retained. They may represent repeated crashes, shared geocoding or rounded locations.
Different identifiers with both the same coordinates and incident timestamp are flagged as possible duplicate reports. I retain them in this initial sample because the compilation does not establish which is the original. Their removal will be checked later.
Records without usable coordinates are excluded from spatial calculations. Those labelled as belonging to the study region remain available for a separate temporal comparison.
Valid coordinates determine spatial membership. Province labels are checked against the polygons rather than used as the initial filter.

I do not move points randomly to make coincident locations disappear. That would change the short distances that the later analysis is meant to investigate.


2.3 Defining space and time
I use the six-province Bangkok and Vicinities grouping documented by Thailand’s National Statistical Office: Bangkok, Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Nakhon Pathom, Samut Prakan and Samut Sakhon. The union of their ADM1 polygons is the study window. This includes suburban and less urbanised land; it is not a boundary of the continuously built-up city.
Coordinates are read as WGS84 longitude/latitude (EPSG:4326) and transformed to WGS84 / UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647). Greater Bangkok lies within this zone, and metre units will support the later distance and bandwidth choices. The six provincial geometries are checked before they are combined.
The temporal window is 1 January 2022 00:00 through 1 January 2023 00:00, exclusive, using incident time. I interpret the timezone-free timestamps as local Thai time (Asia/Bangkok); the source does not explicitly document their timezone. Report time is kept separately and is not substituted for incident time. Monthly comparisons use calendar days as a denominator, so February is not compared with a 31-day month on totals alone. This adjusts for month length, not for traffic exposure.

3.1 Importing without losing the original fields
I use readr to specify the coordinate and count fields explicitly. Accident codes remain text. Parsing dates myself makes the local-time assumption visible. The raw table is retained so that cleaning decisions can be traced back to the downloaded records.

library(sf)

3.2 Building the study window
The boundary uses names such as “Nonthaburi Province”, while the accident table uses “Nonthaburi”. I remove only that suffix for matching and select the six names explicitly. st_union() removes internal provincial borders from the observation window; I keep the separate provinces for mapping and the location audit.

Reading the chart. All 189 missing-coordinate records are labelled Bangkok and belong to the Expressway Authority. A map of the usable records therefore gives an incomplete view of this agency’s reported crash locations. I retain these reports for a temporal comparison, but do not assign them to province centroids or guess which expressways they belong to.

5. Does the monthly pattern depend on the missing locations?
A monthly total is a reasonable first view of timing, but months are not equally long. I divide each total by its number of calendar days. I then add the unlocated Bangkok-labelled reports in a second series. This is a context check: their province labels suggest that they belong in the region, but I cannot verify their locations against the boundary.
Both series use incident month, rather than the month in which a report was entered. The extra reports are never inserted into the spatial objects.

month_calendar <- tibble(month_start = seq(as.Date("2022-01-01"),
                                          as.Date("2022-12-01"), by = "month"))

monthly <- accidents %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(month_start, name = "located_n") %>%
  right_join(month_calendar, by = "month_start") %>%
  left_join(
    unlocated_region %>%
      mutate(month_start = as.Date(floor_date(incident_time, "month"),
                                   tz = "Asia/Bangkok")) %>%
      count(month_start, name = "unlocated_n"),
    by = "month_start"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(located_n, unlocated_n), ~ replace_na(.x, 0L)),
    days = days_in_month(month_start),
    located_per_day = located_n / days,
    including_unlocated_per_day = (located_n + unlocated_n) / days
  ) %>%
  arrange(month_start)

stopifnot(sum(monthly$located_n) == nrow(accidents),
          sum(monthly$unlocated_n) == nrow(unlocated_region), sum(monthly$days) == 365)

monthly %>%
  transmute(Month = month.abb[month(month_start)],
            `Located records` = located_n,
            `Unlocated Bangkok reports` = unlocated_n,
            `Located records per day` = round(located_per_day, 2)) %>%

Changes in travel, reporting or road conditions remain possible explanations to investigate.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: 6. What I have learned so far
text:
6. What I have learned so far
My first concern was whether the map would leave out enough records to affect the story. It does leave out a substantial part of one agency’s Bangkok reports, so that limitation needs to stay visible in later maps. The monthly comparison is a little more reassuring: the late-year rise persists when those reports are included by their province labels.
The map also makes the choice of a reference model important. The observed locations follow roads. Comparing them with points scattered across all land would mix the shape of the road system with the pattern I am trying to understand. The next stage will first examine spatial concentrations at several bandwidths, then ask a narrower second-order question about the association between location and time.
I stop here for this instalment. No density peaks, statistically significant clusters, causal explanation or resource-allocation recommendation have been established. The remaining work is the second- and third-stage analysis set out at the start, followed by a public-safety discussion of at most 500 words and a revealjs summary of at most ten content slides, excluding its cover and contents. title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: 1. What I want to find out
text:
1. What I want to find out
I chose Greater Bangkok because it lets me look at the city together with its surrounding provinces. The 2022 data cover a full calendar year, so I can compare different months within the same period.
There are three questions I want to explore:

Where were most accidents recorded?
Which months had more accidents?
Could missing locations change what the maps and charts show?

I start by checking which records can be used, then look at the locations and timing. A high accident count is a reason to look more closely at an area, but it does not tell us how dangerous it is without knowing how many people travel there.

2. The data



Data
What I use it for




Thailand Road Accident 2019–2022
Accident locations and dates. I use only the records from 2022. Each record describes a reported accident, rather than an individual vehicle or casualty.


Thailand provincial boundaries
Defining the study area and placing accidents within its provinces. These boundaries represent 2017.



Both datasets were downloaded on 11 September 2026. The accident data come from a compilation of Ministry of Transport records covering highways, rural roads and expressways. They do not cover every accident on every local street. Source: Ministry of Transport.
Here, Greater Bangkok means Bangkok, Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Nakhon Pathom, Samut Prakan and Samut Sakhon, following the National Statistical Office’s Bangkok and Vicinities grouping.
I use the date the accident happened, from 1 January to 31 December 2022, rather than the date the report was submitted. I treat the recorded times as local Thai time, although the source does not state the time zone.

3.1 Missing locations
There are 189 records without coordinates. All are listed as accidents in Bangkok. I checked which agency reported them to see whether the missing locations were spread across the data.









All 189 came from the Expressway Authority. They make up 43.1% of its 439 Bangkok reports, compared with no missing locations in the other two agencies’ Bangkok records. This means the map leaves out a substantial part of the Expressway Authority’s reports. I keep these records for the monthly comparison because their dates are still available, but cannot place them on the map.


3.2 Repeated or conflicting locations
Some records share the same location. This can happen when several accidents occur at the same place, so I keep them. Two pairs also share the same accident time but have different record numbers. They may be duplicate reports; the available information is not enough to decide, so they remain in the data.
A few records have coordinates that disagree with their province names. I use their plotted locations to decide whether they belong in the study area. This excludes four records listed under the six provinces and includes ten listed elsewhere. The boundary data are older than the accident records, so I cannot assume every disagreement is a recording error.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
5. When were more accidents recorded?
After looking at where accidents happened, I compare their timing. Simply comparing monthly totals would give longer months more days to accumulate accidents. I therefore divide each month’s total by its number of days.
The solid line uses the records shown on the map. The dashed line adds the 189 reports with missing locations. Their province names place them in Bangkok, although I cannot check their exact positions.









October has the highest count: 394 mapped records, or about 12.7 per day. November has fewer records than December, but more per day because it is a shorter month. April also stands out compared with March and May.
Adding the reports with missing locations raises the figures slightly but leaves the same broad pattern: more accidents were recorded towards the end of the year. The location gaps therefore do not explain that increase on their own. The chart does not tell us whether changes in traffic, road conditions or reporting caused it.
